ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 6 — Focused Visit (Care-plan review) — Paul Robeson

code.originalText: Twenty-four-week review: partial response to venlafaxine; treatment-resistant depression; aripiprazole augmentation and an informed consent discussion about ECT

text.paragraph: Mr. Robeson returns eleven weeks after the switch to venlafaxine; he has taken 225 mg each morning for seven weeks. He sleeps five and a half hours, walks every morning, and has begun to read and see one or two old friends, but he still has little pleasure in music and has not sung in public. The cough from four weeks ago has gone. He sweats a little more than before. He has had no thoughts of suicide since the spring and no elation. He has completed sixteen behavioral activation sessions and continues fortnightly with his psychologist, who reports PHQ-9 scores in the low to mid teens. He asked what else can be done, including whether he would need shock treatment. [S]

list.item:
Treatment-resistant recurrent major depression (F33.2). PHQ-9 22 to 13 after a second adequate trial, of a different class: a partial response without remission, so the depression is treatment-resistant. Sodium 136; blood pressure 134/84, a small rise on venlafaxine that does not need a change. MoCA 28, unchanged. Safety reviewed: no thoughts of suicide; medicines locked; 988 in his phone. Options were discussed with him and with Dr. Lindqvist-Adebayo: augmentation with aripiprazole, lithium or a second antidepressant; ECT; rTMS; and esketamine nasal spray. For ECT, informed consent was discussed as a conversation, not a form: it is given under general anesthesia with a muscle relaxant and monitoring, usually right unilateral with an ultrabrief pulse to limit memory effects, two or three times a week for a defined course of about six to twelve treatments, with cognitive testing before and during the course; its benefits, risks (anesthesia, headache, muscle aches, and memory loss for events around the course) and alternatives were explained, and he was told he could decline or stop at any time. ECT is not needed now: he has no psychosis, is eating and drinking, and is not suicidal, and he chose augmentation first. Black patients receive ECT less often than white patients with the same diagnosis, so the offer stands on equal terms if augmentation fails. rTMS (daily sessions for about six weeks) and esketamine (twice weekly in the clinic, with blood pressure checks) remain alternatives. [S]
Aripiprazole 2 mg each morning, rising to 5 mg in two weeks.
Continue venlafaxine 225 mg.
Weight at four, eight and twelve weeks; A1c and lipids again at twelve weeks; movement examination in six months.

ECT, rTMS or esketamine if there is no clear improvement within about eight weeks, or at once if he becomes unable to eat or drink, psychotic or acutely suicidal.
